items.title: Javon Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I had a conversation with Sonny Rollins about this situation by phone and he said, “Remember there’s always a lot to do in the house.”

ctx.x: As far as loss of gigs and concerts, did your cancellations come all at once or did you sort of see it coming and how did you feel about it when certain engagements you had lined up —

Right, well they came, Monk, as a trickling in the beginning, certain concerts month by month and then there was just several months regarding to the summer just all being cancelled. My reaction is I can’t get mad because everyone is experiencing this, whether in the sports arena, in the performance arena, Broadway theater. So it’s not as if it’s an isolated thing against me, the lone wolf jazz saxophonist, just for everyone. So I just have to kind of accept it and use this opportunity to find some other things…
will come back. But never have I gotten upset about it, because again, everyone is involved in it. Every sect of life.

items.title: Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2010
items.q: Because this person was Sonny Rollins’ first influence, was Louis Jordan, told to me by Sonny.

ctx.x: And I met her through another person, but I said wow. And so I’m quizzing her and I’m talking to her and I’m saying wow. Because this person was Sonny Rollins’ first influence, was Louis Jordan, told to me by Sonny. So it just shows you that all this information is still available to us and we have the music. So I mean sure there’s pros and cons everywhere. There’s organic and there’s this and that, but everyone has to work it out for themselves, to what degree that they want to go out for themselves and try to…
Have you ever had to work a — let’s say from the time you went to Berklee — have you ever had to work a non-music job?
